meta.title: Who really said "Cleanliness is next to godliness"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: It is not in the Bible. “Cleanliness is next to godliness” is an anonymous English proverb, in print by 1773 and popularized by John Wesley.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Cleanliness is next to godliness'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a Bible verse. An 18th-century English proverb, documented in 1773 and made famous by John Wesley, who quoted it as an existing saying.

answer.label: Not in the Bible — an 18th-century English proverb
answer.authorName: John Wesley (popularizer of a pre-existing saying)
answer.sourceLine: The line is not scripture — no verse of the Bible contains it. It is an English proverb of unknown authorship, documented in print by 1773 (Anselm Bayly’s biblical commentary) and popularized by the Methodist founder John Wesley, who in his sermon “On Dress” quoted it as a saying already in circulation: “Cleanliness is, indeed, next to godliness.”

source.heading: Where the proverb actually comes from
source.excerpt: Let it be observed, that slovenliness is no part of religion; that neither this, nor any text of Scripture, condemns neatness of apparel. Certainly this is a duty, not a sin. Cleanliness is, indeed, next to godliness.
trail: Not in the Bible — no verse contains the phrase, as The Phrase Finder and other references confirm.
Earliest documented in print is Anselm Bayly’s 1773 commentary — “Cleanliness, it is rightly said, is next to godliness” — per Word Histories.
John Wesley quoted it in his sermon “On Dress” as “Cleanliness is indeed next to godliness,” collected in Wikiquote’s John Wesley page (Works, 1840 ed.).
source.excerptNote: Wesley’s own wording keeps the interjection “indeed,” and he frames the line as an existing saying — explicitly noting no text of Scripture demands it.

source.rightsNote: The proverb and both its earliest printed forms — Anselm Bayly’s 1773 commentary and John Wesley’s 18th-century sermon “On Dress” — were published well before 1931, so this wording is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: John Wesley
author.heading: About John Wesley
author.bio: John Wesley (1703–1791) was an Anglican cleric and the founder of the Methodist movement, a tireless preacher whose sermons and hymns shaped 18th-century evangelical Christianity. His sermon “On Dress” used the saying “Cleanliness is, indeed, next to godliness” — but he was quoting a proverb already in circulation, not coining it, and he pointedly noted that no text of Scripture makes neatness a religious duty. His fame is why the line is so often misremembered as his own, or as the Bible’s.

misattribution.heading: Who really said it
misattribution.intro: Because it sounds scriptural and moralizing, the line is endlessly cited as a Bible verse. It is not — and even John Wesley, its most famous voice, was quoting someone else.

items.why: The phrase appears nowhere in the Bible; it is a post-biblical English proverb, as The Phrase Finder and Word Histories both note.

Wesley is routinely credited as the source, but in his sermon “On Dress” he quoted it as an existing saying (adding “indeed”), and it was already in print by 1773 — before that sermon — per Word Histories.
Bacon’s Advancement of Learning (1605) voices the sentiment — “cleanness of body was ever esteemed to proceed from a due reverence to God” — but not this wording, per The Phrase Finder.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous English proverb, in print by 1773 and made famous by John Wesley — not a line of scripture, per Word Histories.

context.heading: Why it feels biblical
lead: The proverb pairs physical washing with moral purity in a way that reads like scripture, which is exactly why it gets pinned on the Bible. But the pairing is a cultural inheritance, not a verse: Victorian Christian moralists loved it, and its cadence — “X is next to godliness” — sounds like a psalm.

Ironically, the man who made it famous was warning against reading too much religion into it. Wesley’s point in “On Dress” was that slovenliness is not a sin and neatness is not a scriptural command — cleanliness is merely ‘next to’ godliness, adjacent, not identical.
context.pull: Not in scripture — a proverb Wesley quoted, not coined.
